opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it matters because a lot of people's optimism about the transition to advanced AI quietly rests on it. There's a line of thinking that goes something like: AI systems will be so capable, and potentially so good at reasoning about each other's intentions, that they'll be able to strike deals humans never could. They could verify commitments, read each other's code, credibly bind themselves to agreements, and so escape the prisoner's dilemmas, arms races, and bargaining failures that have plagued human history. If that's true, it changes a lot about how worried we should be about competitive dynamics, about multipolar scenarios, and about conflict.

But I think it's important to examine that hypothesis carefully rather than take it on faith, for a few reasons.

First, cooperative capability is dual-use. The same skills that let agents coordinate to produce public goods also let them collude. Cartels are a form of cooperation. Coalitions that exclude and exploit others are a form of cooperation. So more cooperative capability among AIs, or among the actors controlling them, isn't automatically good for humanity at large. It could just as easily mean very effective coordination among a narrow set of powerful parties.

Second, a lot of conflict isn't fundamentally caused by a lack of intelligence. In the bargaining theory of war, conflict arises from things like private information and incentives to misrepresent it, commitment problems, and indivisible stakes. Some of those might be eased by more capable agents, especially if you get better verification or transparency. But some may get worse. Rapid shifts in power, which advanced AI could produce, are exactly the conditions that create commitment problems. If one side expects to be much stronger next year, it's hard for it to credibly promise not to exploit that advantage, and the other side may have incentives to act preemptively.

Third, there's a question of whether those cooperative capabilities would be available early enough. Even if mature AI systems could in principle solve coordination problems, the critical period might be the transition itself, when systems are powerful enough to be strategically destabilizing but before we have the institutions, verification tools, or trust to make use of them.

So I'd say it matters because it's a load-bearing assumption. If it's right, maybe we can relax somewhat about certain governance problems. If it's wrong, or only partially right, then we need to be actively investing in what I'd call cooperative AI: deliberately building the capabilities, norms, and institutions that steer us toward the beneficial forms of cooperation rather than toward collusion or instability. And I don't think we should just assume intelligence alone gets us there.

r001.rationale: The response says the hypothesis could reduce concern about some governance problems and calls for investing in cooperative AI if it is wrong or incomplete. It does not say that accepting the hypothesis would shift efforts toward safe, aligned AGI instead of directly solving coordination problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it matters because a lot of the big risks we worry about — whether that's arms races in AI itself, or climate, or biosecurity, or great power conflict — are fundamentally coordination problems. They're situations where everyone would be better off if we could all agree to behave in a certain way, but no individual actor can trust that others will hold up their end, so we get stuck in a bad equilibrium. Humanity has been pretty mediocre at solving these problems historically. We've made progress — we have treaties, institutions, norms — but it's slow, fragile, and often fails at exactly the moments when the stakes are highest.

So the question of whether advanced AI could help us do better at cooperation isn't a side issue; it's arguably central to whether the transition to transformative AI goes well. If you think of AGI as primarily amplifying the capabilities of whoever controls it, then you'd naturally expect it to intensify competition — more capable actors racing harder against each other. That's a frightening world. But there's another possibility, which is that advanced AI could lower the costs of the things that make cooperation hard: verifying that the other side is complying, communicating credibly, designing agreements that are robust to defection, even negotiating on behalf of parties who can't easily come to the table themselves.

If that's right, then AI could be a kind of cooperation technology, not just a capability technology. And the reason I think it's worth taking seriously as a hypothesis — rather than just hoping for it — is that it's not automatic. Whether AI ends up strengthening cooperation or eroding it depends a lot on choices we make now: what we build, what we deploy first, what institutions we embed it in. If the hypothesis is true, that tells us there's a tremendous amount of value in deliberately steering toward that outcome. If it's false, we need to know that too, because then we're relying on human institutions to manage a situation far beyond anything they've handled before.

So I'd frame it as: this hypothesis is one of the main hinges on which the long-term outcome turns, and it's underexplored relative to its importance.

r001.rationale: The response says AI might improve cooperation and that this possibility should shape how AI is developed and deployed. It does not say efforts could prioritize developing safe, aligned AGI over directly solving coordination problems.

astra-6.text:
I think it matters because some of the biggest threats we face arise from failures to cooperate. Countries can all prefer a world without a destructive arms race, and yet each country can feel compelled to participate because it doesn’t trust the others to exercise restraint. Being more technologically capable doesn’t automatically resolve that problem. It might just make the race more dangerous.

But intelligence could also help us find agreements that are better for everyone, understand what other parties want, and develop ways to verify that commitments are being kept. If advanced AI could substantially improve those capabilities, it could help us address a whole class of problems, rather than just one particular threat.

The important uncertainty is whether the ability to find cooperative solutions translates into actually implementing them. That depends on incentives, institutions, and how these systems are used. So I wouldn’t assume that AGI solves coordination by default. But the possibility matters enormously: it suggests that AI could help us build a world in which greater capability also means greater collective security.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how AI might help with coordination and notes uncertainty, but it does not say that this possibility should shift efforts toward developing safe, aligned AGI over directly solving coordination problems.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it matters because a lot of the problems we’re worried about aren’t problems of knowing what to do. They’re problems of getting actors with different interests to agree to do it. States might all prefer a world without a dangerous arms race, for example, but each still has incentives to compete, and each is uncertain about what the others will do.

AI could potentially help with that. It could help us understand one another’s preferences, identify agreements that make everyone better off, or develop ways to verify that people are keeping their commitments. So there’s a possibility that increasingly capable AI improves our ability to cooperate, as well as our ability to compete.

But I’d distinguish having the intelligence to find a cooperative solution from having the incentives and institutions to implement it. You don’t automatically solve a bargaining problem just by making everyone smarter. You might also make them better at threatening one another or exploiting an advantage.

So I think this is an important hypothesis to investigate, rather than something to assume. If AI can substantially improve cooperation, that changes the prospects for managing the risks from AI itself, as well as other global problems. And it gives us something constructive to aim for: developing systems that help us reach and sustain agreements we otherwise couldn’t.

r001.rationale: The response says improved AI cooperation could help manage AI risks and provide a constructive development goal, but it does not state that this would prioritize safe, aligned AGI development over directly solving coordination problems.
